topics.title: Predestination & Election
questions: Does God choose who will be saved?
Is election based on foreseen faith?
topics.summary: Both traditions confess that salvation rests on God’s gracious, eternal election in Christ — but they part ways over reprobation.

calvin.answer: Calvin teaches that God, by an eternal and unchangeable decree, chose some to eternal life and passed over others, leaving them to the just condemnation their sin deserves (“double predestination”). The cause of election is not foreseen faith or works but God’s “good pleasure” alone (III.22). Calvin insists the doctrine is humbling and comforting: it shows salvation flows entirely from free mercy. Yet he warns against curious speculation and directs believers to look for their election in Christ, “the mirror” of election, rather than in God’s hidden counsel.
points: Election is unconditional — grounded in God’s will, not foreseen merit.
Reprobation is also part of God’s decree, though the reprobate perish by their own guilt.
Assurance comes by looking to Christ, not by prying into the decree.

quotes.text: By predestination we mean the eternal decree of God, by which he determined with himself whatever he wished to happen with regard to every man. All are not created on equal terms, but some are preordained to eternal life, others to eternal damnation

quotes.text: We shall never feel persuaded as we ought that our salvation flows from the free mercy of God as its fountain, until we are made acquainted with his eternal election

quotes.text: Christ, then, is the mirror in which we ought, and in which, without deception, we may contemplate our election.

lutheran.answer: The Formula of Concord (Art. XI) teaches that God’s eternal election “extends only over the godly, beloved children of God” and is a cause of their salvation, so firmly founded that “the gates of hell cannot overcome it.” But Lutherans reject any decree of reprobation: God does not will the damnation of anyone, and those who perish do so by their own rejection of the Word. Election is not to be searched out in God’s secret counsel but sought in Christ, the Book of Life, through the Gospel and the sacraments. Why some are converted and others not is left as a mystery Scripture does not resolve.
points: Single predestination: election to salvation only, no decree of damnation.
The Gospel promise is meant seriously for all people.
Look for your election in Christ, the Word, and your Baptism — not in God’s hidden will.

compare.summary: Both traditions confess an eternal election by grace in Christ that is the cause of salvation and gives believers comfort. Calvinism follows the logic of the decree to include reprobation (God passes over the non-elect); Lutheranism stops at the biblical tension — God elects to salvation, yet sincerely wills all to be saved, and unbelief alone damns.

Election is in Christ and is meant to comfort, not terrify.
Do not speculate about God’s hidden counsel; look to Christ.

topics.title: Free Will & the Bondage of the Will
questions: Can a person choose to follow God?
What did Luther say to Erasmus?
topics.summary: Both deny that fallen humans can turn to God by their own power; both grant freedom in earthly matters.

calvin.answer: Calvin grants that fallen man acts voluntarily, without compulsion — but denies that he has any power to choose spiritual good. The will is “bound” by sin, so that man sins necessarily yet willingly. Calvin thinks the label “free will” is too proud a title for so small a liberty and prefers to avoid it. Conversion is wholly God’s work: grace does not merely assist a neutral will but creates a new heart.
points: Man sins necessarily, but not by compulsion — willingly.
The term “free will” is misleading and best avoided.
Grace renews the will; it does not merely help it.

quotes.text: In this way, then, man is said to have free will, not because he has a free choice of good and evil, but because he acts voluntarily, and not by compulsion.

lutheran.answer: Augsburg Confession XVIII teaches that the will has “some liberty to choose civil righteousness” but no power, without the Holy Ghost, for spiritual righteousness. The Formula of Concord (II) is blunt: in spiritual things fallen man is “like a pillar of salt… like a log and a stone,” and conversion is solely the Spirit’s work through Word and Sacrament. Luther’s Bondage of the Will (1525), against Erasmus, pictures the will as a beast ridden either by God or by Satan. After conversion, the renewed will does cooperate, by the Spirit’s power.
points: Civil freedom: yes. Spiritual freedom before conversion: none.
Conversion is monergistic — God alone works it through the means of grace.
The renewed believer cooperates by the Spirit’s power, not his own.

topics.title: Original Sin & Total Depravity
topics.summary: Both teach that Adam’s fall corrupted the whole human nature, so that everyone is born guilty and in need of rebirth.

calvin.answer: Calvin defines original sin as “a hereditary corruption and depravity of our nature, extending to all the parts of the soul,” which makes us liable to God’s wrath and produces sinful works. This does not mean humans are as wicked as possible, but that no part of us — mind, will, or affections — is untouched. Later Reformed theology called this “total depravity.”
points: Corruption extends to every faculty of the soul.
It brings guilt as well as corruption.
Remnants of the image of God and natural gifts remain, but spiritual gifts are lost.

quotes.text: Original sin, then, may be defined a hereditary corruption and depravity of our nature, extending to all the parts of the soul, which first makes us obnoxious to the wrath of God, and then produces in us works which in Scripture are termed works of the flesh.

lutheran.answer: Augsburg Confession II confesses that since the fall all born in the natural way “are born with sin, that is, without the fear of God, without trust in God, and with concupiscence,” and that this disease is truly sin, condemning those not born again through Baptism and the Spirit. The Formula of Concord (I) adds an important distinction: original sin is a deep corruption of human nature, but not the very substance of human nature itself — otherwise God would be the creator of sin (against Flacius).

topics.title: Grace, Conversion & Irresistible Grace
questions: How does a person get converted?
topics.summary: Both say conversion is God’s work alone; they differ on whether grace can be successfully resisted.

calvin.answer: Calvin teaches that God’s grace does not offer a mere possibility the will can accept or reject; it effectively renews the heart of the elect. In Institutes II.3 he argues that God “corrects” and “renews” the will, and that what is good in it is entirely God’s work. Later Reformed theology (Dort, 1619) summarized this as “irresistible” or effectual grace — not that people never resist, but that God’s saving purpose for the elect is never ultimately defeated.
points: Grace effectively renews the will of the elect.
The outward call goes to many; the inward, effectual call to the elect.
The term “irresistible grace” is later (Dort), but the idea is in Calvin.

Yet Lutherans teach that grace is resistible: those who perish do so because they stubbornly resist the Spirit, not because God withheld grace from them.

topics.title: Justification by Faith
keywords: article on which the church stands
questions: How is a sinner made right with God?
topics.summary: Near-total agreement: sinners are declared righteous for Christ’s sake, through faith alone, by imputation.

calvin.answer: Calvin calls justification “the principal hinge” of religion (III.11.1). It is a legal declaration: God accepts us “into his favor as if we were righteous,” consisting in forgiveness of sins and the imputation of Christ’s righteousness. Calvin stresses union with Christ: justification and sanctification are distinct but inseparable gifts received together in Christ — “Christ, therefore, justifies no man without also sanctifying him.”
points: Forensic: God declares, rather than infuses, righteousness.
Grounded in Christ’s imputed righteousness alone.
Inseparable from (but not the same as) sanctification.

quotes.text: Thus we simply interpret justification, as the acceptance with which God receives us into his favor as if we were righteous; and we say that this justification consists in the forgiveness of sins and the imputation of the righteousness of Christ

Justification is forensic — the forgiveness of sins and Christ’s righteousness reckoned to the believer.

topics.title: What Is Faith?
topics.summary: For both, faith is not mere intellectual assent but confident trust in God’s promise of mercy in Christ.

calvin.answer: Calvin gives one of the Reformation’s most famous definitions: faith is “a firm and sure knowledge of the divine favor toward us, founded on the truth of a free promise in Christ, and revealed to our minds, and sealed on our hearts, by the Holy Spirit.” Faith involves both mind and heart; it rests on the promise and is the gift of the Spirit. Calvin rejects the scholastic idea of merely “implicit” faith.
points: Knowledge and heartfelt assurance together.
Rests on God’s free promise in Christ.
Created and sealed by the Holy Spirit.

The Apology says this faith “brings to God not confidence in one’s own merits, but only confidence in the promise.” Luther’s Large Catechism explains the First Commandment in terms of faith: “that now… upon which you set your heart and put your trust is properly your god.” Faith is created by the Spirit through the Word and Sacraments.

topics.title: Sanctification & the Christian Life
questions: How does a Christian grow in holiness?
Are Christians saints and sinners at the same time?
topics.summary: Both see holiness as the Spirit’s fruit of justification; Calvin gives it more structural weight, Lutherans guard against making it a ground of assurance.

calvin.answer: For Calvin, union with Christ brings a “double grace”: justification and sanctification. Repentance, which he equates with regeneration, aims “to form in us anew the image of God.” The Christian life is summed up in self-denial: “We are not our own” (III.7.1). Sanctification is progressive and never complete in this life, but it is inseparable from true faith.
points: Repentance = lifelong regeneration restoring God’s image.
Self-denial: we belong to God, not ourselves.
Progressive and imperfect, but real and necessary as fruit.

quotes.text: In one word, then, by repentance I understand regeneration, the only aim of which is to form in us anew the image of God

quotes.text: Christ, therefore, justifies no man without also sanctifying him. These blessings are conjoined by a perpetual and inseparable tie.
quotes.work: Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion (Beveridge tr., 1845)

lutheran.answer: Augsburg Confession VI teaches that faith “is bound to bring forth good fruits,” done because God commands them, not to merit justification. The Christian is simultaneously righteous and a sinner (simul justus et peccator): wholly righteous in Christ, while the old Adam still clings. Sanctification is the Spirit’s work through Word and Sacraments, and daily return to Baptism (Large Catechism) shapes the Christian life of repentance.

Calvin builds a fuller doctrine of the Christian life (self-denial, the law as guide); Lutherans keep the accent on the believer as simultaneously saint and sinner, living from Baptism and the Gospel.

Sanctification is never complete in this life.
Faith and good works cannot be separated.
differ: Calvin: sanctification as a co-equal benefit of union with Christ, with strong use of the Law as guide. Lutheran: sanctification flows from justification; fear of re-introducing works-righteousness is sharper.
Lutherans emphasize daily return to Baptism; Reformed emphasize progress in godliness and self-denial.

topics.title: Good Works
questions: Are good works necessary for salvation?
How do Paul and James fit together?
topics.summary: Both teach that good works follow faith but contribute nothing to justification.

calvin.answer: Calvin teaches that believers are justified apart from works, yet faith is never without works — Christ justifies no one without also sanctifying him. Good works are accepted by God not because they are perfect but because the believer is first accepted in Christ, and God graciously rewards what he himself works in us. James, Calvin argues, speaks of justification as the demonstration of genuine faith before others.
points: Works are excluded from justification but follow faith.
Our works are accepted only because our persons are accepted in Christ.
Rewards are of grace, not merit.

quotes.text: Christ, therefore, justifies no man without also sanctifying him.
quotes.work: Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion (Beveridge tr., 1845)

v: For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;

This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men.
Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.
Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.

lutheran.answer: Augsburg Confession XX defends Lutheran preaching on good works against the charge of forbidding them. The Formula of Concord (IV) affirms good works are necessary as fruits of faith, yet rejects the formula “good works are necessary to salvation,” because it obscures grace and troubles consciences. Luther’s Large Catechism praises everyday duties of one’s calling as “truly golden works,” better than self-chosen religious works.
points: Works are necessary as fruits — not for salvation.
Rejects “good works are necessary to salvation” (FC IV).
God-commanded works in daily vocation are the truly good works.

True faith inevitably produces good works.
God graciously rewards works He Himself produces.

topics.title: Law and Gospel (and the Third Use of the Law)
questions: What is the difference between Law and Gospel?
What is the third use of the law?
Are Christians still under the Ten Commandments?
topics.summary: Both teach three uses of the Law; Calvin calls the third (guide for believers) the principal use, Lutherans keep the Law–Gospel distinction central.

calvin.answer: Calvin describes three uses of the moral Law: it exposes sin like a mirror, restrains the wicked by fear, and — its “principal use” — instructs and exhorts believers in whose hearts the Spirit already reigns. For Calvin the Law is not abolished for Christians as a rule of life; it is freed from its curse. The Law and the Gospel are distinguished, yet both serve the one covenant of grace fulfilled in Christ.
points: Three uses: mirror, curb, guide.
The third use (guide for believers) is the principal one.
Christ removes the Law’s curse, not its authority as a rule of life.

quotes.text: The third use of the Law (being also the principal use, and more closely connected with its proper end) has respect to believers in whose hearts the Spirit of God already flourishes and reigns.

quotes.text: let us take a succinct view of the office and use of the Moral Law. Now this office and use seems to me to consist of three parts.

The Law “is properly a divine doctrine, which teaches what is right and pleasing to God, and reproves everything that is sin”; the Gospel proclaims forgiveness for Christ’s sake. Mixing them either breeds despair or false security. Formula of Concord VI also affirms a third use: the Law should be “diligently urged” upon believers as a mirror of God’s will, because the old Adam still clings to them — yet only the Gospel gives power to obey.

The difference is tone and center: Calvin treats the Law’s guiding role for believers as its principal use; Lutherans make the Law–Gospel distinction the hermeneutical key and stress that “the Law always accuses” even believers.

The Law cannot justify; only the Gospel saves.
Believers still need the Law’s instruction.

topics.title: Assurance of Salvation
questions: How can I know I am saved?
What if I doubt my election?
topics.summary: Both point the troubled conscience away from itself to Christ; Lutherans add the objective anchors of Baptism and the Supper.

calvin.answer: Calvin teaches that assurance belongs to the nature of faith: faith is a “firm and sure knowledge of the divine favor.” Believers still struggle with doubt, but true faith is never extinguished. Against anxious speculation about the decree, Calvin points to Christ: he is the mirror in which we may contemplate our election without deception. Good works can confirm assurance as signs of God’s grace, but never as its foundation.
points: Assurance is of the essence of faith, though often assailed.
Look to Christ, not into the secret decree.
Works are secondary confirmations, not the ground.

quotes.text: Christ, then, is the mirror in which we ought, and in which, without deception, we may contemplate our election.
quotes.work: Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion (Beveridge tr., 1845)

quotes.text: a firm and sure knowledge of the divine favor toward us, founded on the truth of a free promise in Christ
quotes.work: Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion (Beveridge tr., 1845)

These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life, and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.

For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day.

lutheran.answer: Lutherans direct anxious consciences to external, objective promises: the preached Word, Holy Absolution, Baptism, and the Lord’s Supper. The Formula of Concord (XI) warns against harassing oneself with thoughts about God’s secret counsel; instead one should “hear Christ,” who is the Book of Life. Because Baptism is God’s own work, the Christian can cling to it in every temptation.

Baptism, Absolution and the Supper are concrete pledges.
Don’t search the hidden will of God; hear Christ.

Look to Christ, not God’s hidden counsel.

topics.title: Perseverance — Can a Christian Fall Away?
questions: Can a Christian lose their salvation?
What does the perseverance of the saints mean?
topics.summary: A clear difference: Calvin teaches the elect cannot finally fall; Lutherans confess that true believers can fall from grace.

calvin.answer: Calvin teaches that those whom God has truly elected and united to Christ will persevere to the end, because perseverance is God’s gift and his purpose cannot fail (III.24.6–7; II.3.11). Apparent believers who fall away were never truly ingrafted into Christ, though they may have shown signs of grace. This became the “P” of later Reformed teaching (Dort).
points: The elect are kept by God to the end.
Perseverance is a gift of grace, not human strength.
Those who finally fall away were never truly united to Christ.

quotes.text: Christ, then, is the mirror in which we ought, and in which, without deception, we may contemplate our election.
quotes.work: Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion (Beveridge tr., 1845)

v: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:
And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all; and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father’s hand.
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.

They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out , that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us.
And this is the Father’s will which hath sent me, that of all which he hath given me I should lose nothing, but should raise it up again at the last day.

Institutes II.3.11: perseverance is a free gift of God.

lutheran.answer: Lutherans teach both God’s faithful preservation of the elect and the real possibility that believers can fall from grace through unbelief or impenitent sin. Augsburg Confession XII condemns those “who deny that those once justified can lose the Holy Ghost.” Yet the fallen can be restored through repentance. The Formula of Concord also confesses that the salvation of the elect is founded so firmly “that the gates of hell cannot overcome it.” Lutherans hold both truths without resolving them rationally.

The fallen may be restored by repentance.
God’s election of His children is nevertheless certain.

topics.title: Atonement & Its Extent
questions: What did Christ accomplish on the cross?
topics.summary: Both teach Christ’s substitutionary satisfaction for sin; they differ over for whom it was intended.

calvin.answer: Calvin teaches that Christ, as our substitute, bore the curse and the wrath of God, expiating our sins by his sacrifice; in his descent into hell “he bore in his soul the tortures of condemned and ruined man.” But Christ’s benefits profit us only through union with him by the Spirit and faith. The formal doctrine of “limited” or definite atonement was articulated later (Synod of Dort, 1619); scholars debate how exactly Calvin himself would have stated the extent question, since he also speaks freely of Christ offered to the whole world.
points: Penal substitution: Christ bore our curse and God’s wrath.
The benefits are applied only through Spirit-wrought union with Christ.
“Limited atonement” as a formula comes from Dort; Calvin’s own view is debated.

quotes.text: he bore in his soul the tortures of condemned and ruined man.

quotes.work: Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion (Beveridge tr., 1845)

The Formula of Concord (XI) teaches that God earnestly calls all sinners to himself. Those who are lost are lost not because Christ did not die for them but because they reject the grace offered.

Universal: Christ died for all people.
Unbelief, not a limited atonement, is why some perish.

topics.title: The Sacraments (What They Are & How Many)
topics.summary: Both count Baptism and the Supper (Lutherans sometimes Absolution) and reject Rome’s seven; they differ on how sacraments convey grace.

calvin.answer: Calvin defines a sacrament as “an external sign, by which the Lord seals on our consciences his promises of good-will toward us, in order to sustain the weakness of our faith.” Sacraments are attached to the Word; they truly offer Christ, but “duly perform their office only when accompanied by the Spirit.” Calvin recognizes two sacraments, Baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and rejects the five additional Roman sacraments (IV.19).
points: Sign and seal of God’s promise, joined to the Word.
Effective only by the Spirit’s inner working, received by faith.
Two sacraments: Baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

quotes.text: The sacraments duly perform their office only when accompanied by the Spirit, the internal Master

questions: Can we have images of Jesus?

topics.summary: Calvin restricts worship to what God commands and opposes images in worship; Lutherans keep edifying traditions and images as adiaphora.

calvin.answer: Calvin sees the human mind as “a perpetual forge of idols” and holds that God must be worshipped only as He has appointed in His Word (an idea later called the regulative principle). Any image of God is forbidden; only visible things may be painted or sculptured, and even those should not be used in worship. Calvin opposed images in churches and stripped worship of human-invented ceremonies.

Is God the author of sin?
topics.summary: Both confess God’s providential care and deny He is the author of sin; Calvin presses God’s ordaining will further.

calvin.answer: Calvin teaches a meticulous providence: nothing happens by chance — “not a drop of rain falls without the express command of God.” God governs even the actions of the wicked, yet remains free from every taint of sin (I.18). On the fall, Calvin says: “Man therefore falls, divine providence so ordaining, but he falls by his own fault.” He calls ignorance of providence “the greatest of all miseries,” and knowledge of it the highest happiness, because it frees believers from fear.
points: Nothing happens by chance; God governs all things.
God ordains even evil events yet is not the author of sin.
Providence is meant to comfort believers.

topics.title: Church & State / Two Kingdoms
questions: How should Christians relate to government?
What is the two kingdoms doctrine?
topics.summary: Both distinguish spiritual and civil government and honor magistrates; Calvin gives the magistrate a stronger role in upholding true religion.

calvin.answer: Calvin teaches “a twofold government in man”: the spiritual, relating to eternal life, and the civil, regulating outward conduct. The spiritual kingdom of Christ and civil government are “things very widely separated,” yet not opposed; magistracy is a calling approved by God, and its duties include protecting the outward worship of God. Obedience is owed even to bad rulers, but only so far as it is compatible with God’s Word: “We ought to obey God rather than men.” Calvin also allowed lesser magistrates to restrain tyranny (IV.20.31).

Magistracy is a godly calling, including care for true religion.

questions: Why should we pray if God is sovereign?
What is the Lord’s Prayer about?
topics.summary: Both see prayer as faith’s chief exercise, commanded by God and grounded in His promises through Christ.

calvin.answer: Calvin’s longest chapter (III.20, 52 sections) treats prayer as “a perpetual exercise of faith.” We pray not to inform God but to stir up our own hearts, to receive His promised benefits, and to grow in gratitude. He gives rules for right prayer: reverence, sincere sense of need, humility, and confident hope — always through Christ the only Mediator.
points: Prayer is the chief exercise of faith.
It trains our hearts; God does not need informing.
Through Christ alone, with reverence, humility and confidence.

topics.title: Christian Liberty & Vocation
questions: Does my ordinary job matter to God?
What is the priesthood of all believers?
topics.summary: Both teach freedom of conscience in Christ and the dignity of everyday callings.

calvin.answer: Calvin treats Christian liberty in three parts (III.19): believers look to Christ alone for righteousness, not the Law; they obey God willingly, not from legal compulsion; and they use “indifferent” things with a free conscience. On vocation, Calvin says “the Lord enjoins every one of us, in all the actions of life, to have respect to our own calling,” so that no work, however humble, is sordid if done in obedience to God (III.10.6).
points: Liberty: freedom from the Law’s curse, willing obedience, free use of indifferent things.
Every lawful calling is assigned by God.
Humble work is precious in God’s sight.

quotes.text: the Lord enjoins every one of us, in all the actions of life, to have respect to our own calling.
quotes.work: Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion (Beveridge tr., 1845)

v: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.
Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called.
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ.
I know, and am persuaded by the Lord Jesus, that there is nothing unclean of itself: but to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean.

lutheran.answer: Luther’s Concerning Christian Liberty (1520) opens with a famous paradox: “A Christian man is the most free lord of all, and subject to none; a Christian man is the most dutiful servant of all, and subject to every one.” Free by faith, the Christian serves the neighbor in love. In his Address to the Christian Nobility Luther taught that “we are all consecrated as priests by baptism,” and that “a cobbler, a smith, a peasant, every man has the office and function of his calling.” The Large Catechism calls faithful service in one’s station “truly golden works.”

Priesthood of all baptized believers.
Every honest calling is a holy vocation.

topics.title: Repentance, Confession & Absolution
questions: Should Christians confess to a pastor?
topics.summary: Both reject Roman penance; Lutherans retain private confession and absolution as a precious gift, Calvin allows it as voluntary.

calvin.answer: Calvin defines repentance broadly as lifelong regeneration — “by repentance I understand regeneration” — consisting of mortification of the flesh and vivification by the Spirit. He rejects compulsory enumeration of sins to a priest, but grants that confessing to one another (James 5:16) and seeking counsel and comfort from a pastor are useful and voluntary (III.4.6–14).

No obligatory auricular confession.
Voluntary confession to a pastor may comfort the troubled.

topics.title: Ministry, Ordination & the Papacy
questions: Who may preach and administer the sacraments?
topics.summary: Both require a regular call to the public ministry and reject papal supremacy; they differ on church order.

calvin.answer: Calvin teaches that God rules his Church through the ministry of men, and despising that ministry is despising God’s own instruction (IV.1.5; IV.3). He identifies four offices from Scripture — pastors, teachers (doctors), elders, and deacons — and treats bishops, presbyters and pastors as the same office in the New Testament. No one should take the office without a lawful call. Calvin rejects papal primacy and, following Paul and Daniel, saw the Roman papacy as the seat of Antichrist (IV.2.12; IV.7).
points: Ministry of men is God’s ordinary way of teaching His Church.
Fourfold office: pastors, teachers, elders, deacons.
Papal supremacy rejected.

quotes.text: whose perverseness cannot submit to the yoke of being taught by the lips and ministry of men.

topics.title: Christ’s Descent into Hell

topics.summary: Both keep the creedal article but interpret it differently: Calvin as Christ’s soul-suffering on the cross, Lutherans as His victorious proclamation.

calvin.answer: Calvin argues that the creed’s “descended into hell” is not a mere repetition of “buried.” He interprets it as the invisible, spiritual agony Christ endured before God in our place: “not only was the body of Christ given up as the price of redemption, but… he bore in his soul the tortures of condemned and ruined man.” The descent is part of Christ’s humiliation and satisfaction.
points: Not a repeat of “buried.”
Christ endured God’s wrath in His soul for us.
Part of His humiliation and atoning work.

topics.title: Sabbath & the Lord’s Day
topics.summary: Both see the ceremonial Sabbath fulfilled in Christ while keeping a day for hearing God’s Word; later Reformed Puritans became stricter.

calvin.answer: Calvin (II.8.28–34) teaches that the Sabbath’s ceremonial aspect was abolished by Christ, but its purposes endure: spiritual rest from our works so God may work in us, gathering to hear the Word and worship, and rest for servants and workers. The Lord’s Day is observed “without Judaism,” as a matter of good order rather than superstitious necessity. (Later English Puritans adopted a stricter Sabbatarian view than Calvin’s.)

lutheran.answer: Luther’s Large Catechism explains that the Sabbath commandment “according to its gross sense, does not concern us Christians,” since the external day-observance was a Jewish ordinance. Its Christian meaning is that we sanctify the day of rest by occupying ourselves with God’s Word; Sunday is kept for that purpose and for bodily rest, not as a binding ceremonial law. AC XXVIII adds that the Church did not make Sunday necessary by divine law.

compare.summary: Calvin and Luther are close: neither binds Christians to the Jewish Sabbath, both keep the Lord’s Day for the Word and rest. The later strict “Christian Sabbath” of Puritan and Westminster theology goes beyond Calvin himself.

Later Reformed (Westminster) Sabbatarianism is stricter than either.
